# Bylda — full answers

> Bylda is behavioral sales intelligence: it analyzes recorded sales calls, detects rep and buyer behaviors (objections, pacing, questioning, control, next steps), and tells managers which calls and reps need attention and reps what to change — without anyone listening to every call. Findings are associations between behavior and outcomes, not proof of cause. Bylda is in early access.

Source: https://usebylda.com/questions · Updated 2026-09-24

## Why deals are lost or stall

### Why do sales reps lose deals?

Most deals are lost in specific, repeatable moments inside the conversation: pricing introduced before the buyer’s problem is clear, an objection answered instead of investigated, a decision maker who never joins, or a call that ends without a booked next step. CRM loss reasons rarely capture these, because they’re chosen after the fact from a dropdown.

More: https://usebylda.com/deal-intelligence

### How do you find out why sales deals stall?

Look at the last two or three conversations before the stall, not the stage history. Check whether the next step was booked with a date, whether the economic buyer ever attended, whether an objection was raised and left unresolved, and whether the buyer’s questions stopped. Stalls usually show up in behavior weeks before they show up in the pipeline.

More: https://usebylda.com/blog/how-to-identify-a-deal-at-risk

### What is deal slippage, and how do you prevent it?

Deal slippage is when an opportunity’s close date keeps moving to later periods. It’s prevented earlier than most teams try: by confirming the decision process and who signs before pricing, booking every next step with a date and owner, and catching the calls where control shifted to the buyer — “send me something” with nothing scheduled.

More: https://usebylda.com/deal-intelligence

### Why do prospects go quiet after a demo?

Prospects usually go quiet when the demo answered questions they hadn’t asked yet. Common patterns: discovery was cut short, the demo covered features rather than the problem the buyer described, and the call ended with a follow-up email instead of a scheduled decision step. The fix is in the call before the demo, not the chase afterward.

More: https://usebylda.com/demo-call-analysis

### How do you tell from a sales call that a deal is at risk?

Listen for behavior, not sentiment: the buyer stops asking questions, a new approver appears late, pricing is challenged and the rep rushes past it, stakeholders who were on earlier calls stop attending, or the rep accepts “send me something” without setting a date. One of these is a moment; several repeating across calls is a risk pattern.

More: https://usebylda.com/deal-intelligence

### What does “send me something” mean on a sales call?

“Send me something” usually means the buyer is ending the conversation politely without committing to a next step. It’s often associated with deals that stall. A stronger response is to agree, then ask what they’d need to see to decide and book a time to review it together, so control of the next step stays shared.

More: https://usebylda.com/pricing-call-analysis

## Coaching without listening to every call

### How can a sales manager review calls without listening to all of them?

Stop sampling and start filtering. Use software that analyzes every recorded call for specific behaviors — objections, pacing, discovery depth, next steps — and surfaces the few calls and reps where something is repeating. The manager then listens to the flagged moments, at the timestamp, instead of hunting through whole recordings.

More: https://usebylda.com/for-sales-managers

### How many sales calls should a manager review each week?

Most managers can realistically review three to five full calls a week, which is a small fraction of what a team of eight reps produces. The number matters less than which calls: coaching from a random sample misses the patterns that repeat in the calls nobody hears. Prioritize calls where a known behavior repeated.

More: https://usebylda.com/for-sales-managers

### What should a sales manager coach first?

Coach the behavior that repeats most across a rep’s recent calls and appears most often before lost or stalled deals — one thing at a time. A rep given five things to fix usually fixes none. Tie the coaching to two or three specific call moments so the rep can hear exactly what changed.

More: https://usebylda.com/ai-sales-coaching

### How do you coach reps on objection handling?

Start from real calls, not scripts. Find the moments where the rep answered an objection immediately, then compare them with calls where the rep paused, acknowledged the concern and asked one diagnostic question. Practice that specific sequence, then check the rep’s next real calls to see whether it held under pressure.

More: https://usebylda.com/objection-handling-analysis

### Does call scoring improve sales performance?

A score on its own rarely changes behavior, because it doesn’t tell the rep what to do differently. Scores are useful for trends; coaching needs the specific moment and the better move. Reps improve faster from “you speed up when price comes up — pause and ask one question” than from “67 out of 100.”

More: https://usebylda.com/for-sales-reps

### How do you give sales reps feedback that changes behavior?

Make it specific, timestamped and singular: one behavior, the call moments that show it, and a concrete alternative to try. Let the rep see their own findings first, then check their next real calls to confirm the change. Feedback tied to evidence the rep can replay is far harder to dismiss than opinion.

More: https://usebylda.com/for-sales-reps

## Measuring sales behavior

### What sales behaviors are associated with winning deals?

It differs by team and market, which is why generic benchmarks mislead. Behaviors worth measuring in your own won and lost deals include discovery depth before pricing, whether decision criteria were confirmed, how objections were handled, whether the signer attended, and whether every call ended with a scheduled next step. Compare your own outcomes, not someone else’s averages.

More: https://usebylda.com/behavioral-sales-intelligence

### How do you measure discovery call quality?

Measure what happened, not how long it lasted: how many open questions were asked, whether the rep followed up on answers, whether the buyer described a consequence of doing nothing, whether decision criteria and process were covered, and whether pricing waited until after. Compare these across calls that did and didn’t progress.

More: https://usebylda.com/discovery-call-analysis

### How do you track objection handling across a sales team?

Tag each objection by type — price, timing, authority, competitor, status quo — then record what the rep did next: answered immediately, acknowledged, or asked a diagnostic question, and how long they spoke afterward. Tracked across the team, this shows which objections are rising and which responses appear before deals that progress.

More: https://usebylda.com/objection-handling-analysis

### What is a good talk-to-listen ratio in sales?

There isn’t one universal number, and commonly cited benchmarks vary by call type — discovery calls need more listening than demos. A more useful question is when the rep talks: long monologues right after an objection or a pricing question are a stronger warning sign than the overall ratio. Compare ratios against your own winning calls.

More: https://usebylda.com/conversation-intelligence

### Does a rep’s speaking pace matter on sales calls?

Pace matters most when it changes. Many reps speed up under pressure — after a price objection, for example — and that shift is more telling than their average pace. A sudden increase often comes with interruptions and over-explaining, and it’s one of the easiest behaviors for a rep to fix once they can see it.

More: https://usebylda.com/for-sales-reps

### How do you measure MEDDPICC adherence on calls?

Check each call for evidence of each element — metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, paper process, identified pain, champion and competition — rather than relying on CRM fields reps fill in afterward. The useful view is which elements are skipped most often, by which reps, and in which deals that later stalled.

More: https://usebylda.com/meddpicc-call-analysis

## Conversation intelligence vs. behavioral intelligence

### What is conversation intelligence?

Conversation intelligence is software that records, transcribes and indexes sales calls, then reports on what was said — topics, keywords, talk ratios and trackers. It makes calls searchable and reviewable. The interpretation — what the pattern means and what a rep should change — is usually left to the manager.

More: https://usebylda.com/conversation-intelligence

### What is behavioral sales intelligence?

Behavioral sales intelligence analyzes how reps and buyers behave in sales conversations — objections, questioning, pacing, control, next steps — finds which behaviors repeat across a team, and connects them to the outcomes that followed. It tells managers what to coach and reps what to change, without anyone listening to every call.

More: https://usebylda.com/behavioral-sales-intelligence

### What’s the difference between conversation intelligence and behavioral intelligence?

Conversation intelligence reports what was said; behavioral intelligence explains what was done and whether it matters. The first returns searchable calls and metrics for a manager to interpret. The second treats each call as one sample, finds behaviors that repeat across the team, and returns a specific recommendation with the moments that justify it.

More: https://usebylda.com/conversation-intelligence

### What is revenue intelligence?

Revenue intelligence aggregates CRM, activity and pipeline data to forecast revenue and flag at-risk deals. It answers which deals are at risk and what the number will be. It generally doesn’t explain the behavior inside the calls that caused the risk, which is where behavioral intelligence focuses.

More: https://usebylda.com/clari-alternative

### Do you need Gong to improve sales coaching?

Not necessarily. A call recorder with search is useful if managers have time to review calls. If the bottleneck is that nobody can listen to enough calls, the need is analysis that tells managers which calls and behaviors matter. Some teams run both: a recorder as the library, behavioral intelligence as the coach.

More: https://usebylda.com/gong-alternative

### What are alternatives to Gong for sales coaching?

Alternatives fall into three groups: other conversation intelligence platforms that record and index calls, revenue intelligence platforms focused on forecasting, and behavioral intelligence tools like Bylda that analyze recorded calls to recommend what each rep should change. Choose by the job: a searchable library, a forecast, or coaching priorities.

More: https://usebylda.com/gong-alternative

## AI, data and trust

### Can AI analyze sales calls accurately?

AI is reliable at observable conduct — who spoke when, questions asked, interruptions, pace, whether pricing or next steps came up — and less reliable when it infers feelings or intent. The trustworthy approach is to report conduct, link every finding to the exact timestamp, and let people verify it by listening.

More: https://usebylda.com/ai-sales-call-analysis

### Does AI sales coaching actually work?

It works when it produces one specific, evidence-backed change per rep and checks whether that change showed up in later calls. It doesn’t work when it generates generic advice — “ask more open questions” — from a single transcript. The test is whether rep behavior on real calls changes, not whether the advice sounds right.

More: https://usebylda.com/ai-sales-coaching

### Can AI detect emotion or sentiment on sales calls?

Some tools claim to, but inferring emotion from voice is contested science and increasingly restricted in workplace settings. Bylda deliberately doesn’t score emotion. It reports observable conduct — what was said, when, and in what order — which is measurable, verifiable at a timestamp, and something a rep can actually change.

More: https://usebylda.com/behavioral-sales-intelligence

### Is it legal to record and analyze sales calls?

Generally yes, when participants are properly notified and consent rules are followed — some jurisdictions require every party to consent. Analysis should follow the same consent your recording tool captures. Check the rules where you and your buyers are located; this isn’t legal advice.

More: https://usebylda.com/security

### Will sales reps feel monitored by call analysis?

They will if the tool behaves like surveillance: leaderboards, manager-first access and personality scores. Adoption is better when reps see their own findings first, findings describe conduct rather than character, and every claim links to a moment they can replay and disagree with.

More: https://usebylda.com/for-sales-reps

### Can AI update the CRM automatically from sales calls?

Yes. AI can extract structured facts from a call — next steps, stakeholders, timeline, objections, budget signals — and write them to CRM fields, with each value traceable to the moment it came from. The value is accuracy the record never had when reps typed it from memory.

More: https://usebylda.com/crm-automation

## About Bylda

### What is Bylda?

Bylda is behavioral sales intelligence. It analyzes your team’s recorded sales calls, detects rep and buyer behaviors — objections, pacing, questioning, control, next steps — and shows managers which calls and reps need attention and reps what to change, without anyone listening to every call.

More: https://usebylda.com/

### How is Bylda different from Gong?

Gong is a mature conversation and revenue intelligence platform built around a searchable call library and forecasting. Bylda focuses on behavior: it finds what repeats across a team’s calls, links it to the moments behind it, and returns specific coaching priorities, then checks whether behavior changed. Many teams would use them for different jobs.

More: https://usebylda.com/gong-alternative

### What does Bylda need to get started?

Recorded sales calls and, ideally, a connected CRM. Bylda works from the recordings your team already makes and the CRM you already use, so reps don’t change how they work. Early-access teams start with one week of calls.

More: https://usebylda.com/how-it-works

### How long does it take to see behavioral patterns?

Individual call findings are available as soon as calls are analyzed. Patterns — the same behavior repeating across calls or reps — typically need at least a week of a team’s conversations. Relationships to outcomes take longer, because deals need time to close or stall.

More: https://usebylda.com/how-it-works

### Does Bylda replace the CRM?

No. The CRM stays your system of record. Bylda reads it for context and can write conversation context back to it, while adding the behavioral layer the CRM was never designed to hold.

More: https://usebylda.com/crm-automation

### How much does Bylda cost?

Bylda is priced per rep per month, with plans for teams and custom pricing for larger organizations. Current plans are on the pricing page; Bylda is in early access, onboarding teams in small groups.

More: https://usebylda.com/pricing

## Call analysis guides

### MEDDPICC call analysis

MEDDPICC call analysis is the practice of checking recorded sales conversations for evidence of each qualification element — Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Paper process, Identified pain, Champion and Competition — instead of trusting CRM fields reps complete after the call.

What Bylda tracks:
- Which elements were evidenced on the call, with the timestamp
- Elements marked complete in the CRM but never discussed
- Which reps skip which elements most often
- Elements most often missing in deals that later stalled
- Whether pricing was discussed before decision criteria

Common breakdowns:
- Economic buyer assumed, never met: The champion speaks for the signer. The signer never attends a call.
- Paper process discovered at the end: Procurement, security and legal steps appear after the verbal yes.
- Pain stated, never quantified: The buyer names a problem; the call never establishes what it costs.

**What does MEDDPICC stand for?** Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Paper process, Identified pain, Champion and Competition — a qualification framework for complex B2B sales.

**How do you know if reps are really using MEDDPICC?** Check the calls, not the CRM. Fields are often completed from memory or optimism. Evidence in the conversation — the buyer describing their decision process, the signer attending — is what shows the element was actually covered.

**Which MEDDPICC element is skipped most often?** It varies by team, which is the point of measuring it. Economic buyer access and paper process are frequently assumed rather than confirmed, and both tend to surface late in deals that slip.

**Does Bylda replace MEDDPICC training?** No. It shows where the framework breaks down in real calls, so training and coaching can focus on the elements your team actually skips.

Page: https://usebylda.com/meddpicc-call-analysis

### Challenger call analysis

Challenger call analysis measures whether sales conversations show the three Challenger behaviors — teaching a new perspective, tailoring it to the buyer’s situation, and taking control of the conversation and next steps — and where those behaviors break down.

What Bylda tracks:
- Whether an insight was shared before the pitch
- Whether the insight referenced the buyer’s own situation
- What the rep did after the buyer pushed back — held, reframed or retreated
- Who set the next step, and whether it had a date
- Changes in pace and interruptions under pressure

Common breakdowns:
- Teaching turns into pitching: The insight is delivered as product features instead of a new view of the buyer’s problem.
- Retreat after pushback: The buyer challenges the reframe and the rep immediately agrees and moves on.
- Control handed back at the end: The buyer sets the next step, often “send me something.”

**What are the three Challenger behaviors?** Teach — share an insight that changes how the buyer sees their problem; tailor — connect it to their situation and stakeholders; take control — lead the conversation, including pricing and next steps.

**Where does Challenger most often break down?** Frequently right after the buyer pushes back. Reps trained to challenge often retreat under live pressure, which shows up as a quick concession, faster speech and a next step set by the buyer.

**Can you measure “taking control” objectively?** Partly. Observable signs include who proposes the next step, whether it has a date and owner, whether the rep asks for commitment, and whether pricing is discussed on the rep’s terms.

**Does Bylda work with other methodologies too?** Yes. Bylda measures observable conduct, so the same analysis applies to MEDDPICC, SPIN, NEPQ or your own process.

Page: https://usebylda.com/challenger-sale-call-analysis

### NEPQ call analysis

NEPQ call analysis checks whether sales conversations follow the Neuro-Emotional Persuasion Questioning flow — connecting, situation, problem-awareness, solution-awareness, consequence and commitment questions — and where reps skip stages or start presenting too early.

What Bylda tracks:
- Which question stages appeared, in what order
- How long the rep stayed in problem-awareness before presenting
- Whether consequence questions were asked at all
- Rep talk time after the buyer admits a problem
- Whether the call closed on a commitment question

Common breakdowns:
- Pitching at the first admission: The buyer names a problem and the rep starts presenting immediately.
- Consequence skipped: The cost of doing nothing is never explored, so urgency never forms.
- Commitment never asked: The call ends on interest rather than a decision.

**What is NEPQ in sales?** Neuro-Emotional Persuasion Questioning, a question-led selling approach where the rep guides the buyer to articulate their own problem, its consequences and the change they want before presenting a solution.

**What’s the most common NEPQ mistake on calls?** Moving to the pitch as soon as the buyer admits a problem, skipping consequence questions that build urgency.

**Can software tell which question stage a rep is in?** It can classify questions by purpose and order with reasonable reliability, and every classification links to the timestamp so it can be checked.

**Is NEPQ better than other methodologies?** That depends on your market. The useful question is whether your team executes the method you chose — and whether doing so is associated with better outcomes in your own deals.

Page: https://usebylda.com/nepq-call-analysis

### Discovery call analysis

Discovery call analysis reviews first and early sales conversations for the depth and order of questioning — situation, problem, consequence, decision criteria and process — and whether the rep followed up on answers before moving to a pitch or pricing.

What Bylda tracks:
- Number and type of questions, and how many were followed up
- Whether the buyer described the cost of doing nothing
- Whether decision criteria and process were confirmed
- When pricing came up relative to discovery
- Whether the call ended with a scheduled next step

Common breakdowns:
- The questionnaire call: Many questions, no follow-up — the rep collects answers without going deeper.
- Pricing too early: The buyer asks for a number and the rep gives one before criteria are known.
- No consequence: The problem is named but never sized, so there’s nothing to justify change.

**What makes a good discovery call?** Open questions that get followed up, a problem the buyer describes in their own words, an understanding of what it costs them to do nothing, a confirmed decision process — and a scheduled next step.

**How many questions should a rep ask on a discovery call?** There’s no magic number. Follow-up matters more than count: eleven questions with no follow-up often uncover less than six that each go a level deeper.

**When should pricing come up in discovery?** Usually after the problem, its cost and the decision criteria are understood. Early pricing isn’t always wrong, but it’s worth checking how often it appears before deals stall in your own data.

**How do you measure discovery quality at scale?** Analyze every discovery call for the same observable markers and compare calls that progressed with those that didn’t, rather than reviewing a handful by hand.

Page: https://usebylda.com/discovery-call-analysis

### Demo call analysis

Demo call analysis reviews product demonstration calls for how closely the demo followed the problems the buyer described in discovery, how much of the call was rep monologue, how the buyer engaged, and whether the call ended with a decision step.

What Bylda tracks:
- Which features shown map to problems the buyer described
- Longest uninterrupted rep monologue
- When buyer questions started — and stopped
- Who attended versus who needs to decide
- How the call ended: scheduled decision step or vague follow-up

Common breakdowns:
- The feature tour: Everything the product does, instead of the three things this buyer needs.
- The disappearing buyer: Questions stop halfway through; the rep keeps presenting.
- No decision step: The call ends on interest, not on who decides what by when.

**Why do sales demos fail to convert?** Commonly because the demo covers features the buyer didn’t ask about, runs as a long monologue, happens before discovery was complete, or ends without a scheduled decision step.

**How long should a sales demo be?** Long enough to show what solves the buyer’s stated problems — often shorter than reps think. Watch for when the buyer stops asking questions; that’s usually where attention ended.

**What should happen at the end of a demo?** Agreement on what the buyer needs to decide, who else must be involved, and a scheduled next step with a date.

**Can you analyze screen-share demos?** Bylda analyzes the conversation — who spoke, what was asked and how the call ended — from the recording your conferencing tool already captures.

Page: https://usebylda.com/demo-call-analysis

### Pricing call analysis

Pricing call analysis examines the moments in sales conversations where price is introduced or challenged — how quickly the rep responds, how long they speak afterward, whether the concern is investigated, whether a discount is offered unprompted, and who sets the next step.

What Bylda tracks:
- Response latency after a price objection
- Change in speaking pace and length of the reply
- Whether the rep asked what’s behind the concern
- Unprompted discounts or option-stacking
- Who set the next step after pricing, and whether it had a date

Common breakdowns:
- The instant defense: The rep justifies the price before understanding the objection.
- Option-stacking: Smaller rollout, annual plan, onboarding included — offered in one breath.
- The polite exit: “Send me something” — and the rep agrees without a date.

**How should reps respond to a price objection?** Pause, acknowledge the concern, and ask one diagnostic question — “too much compared to what?” — before offering options. The answer tells you whether it’s budget, value or timing.

**Why do reps discount too early?** Often because the objection is treated as a negotiation instead of a question. Discounts offered before the concern is understood are frequently unnecessary.

**Is it bad to discuss pricing early?** Not always. It’s worth checking whether early pricing in your own deals comes before decision criteria are known — that sequence is often associated with stalls.

**Can Bylda detect when a rep rushes?** Yes — response latency, pace changes and reply length after an objection are observable in the recording and each links to the timestamp.

Page: https://usebylda.com/pricing-call-analysis

### Objection handling analysis

Objection handling analysis tracks the objections buyers raise across a team’s sales calls — price, timing, authority, competitor, status quo — and measures how reps respond: speed, length, whether the concern was investigated, and what happened next in the deal.

What Bylda tracks:
- Objections by type, trend and rep
- Response behavior: immediate answer, acknowledgement, diagnostic question
- Reply length and pace after each objection
- Objections left unresolved at the end of the call
- Which responses appear before deals that progress

Common breakdowns:
- Answering the wrong objection: The rep responds to the stated objection instead of the concern underneath it.
- Winning the argument, losing the deal: Long, well-reasoned rebuttals that end the buyer’s engagement.
- Unresolved and forgotten: The objection is raised, parked and never returned to.

**What are the most common sales objections?** Price, timing (“not right now”), authority (“I need to check with…”), competitor and status quo (“we’re fine with what we have”). Which dominates varies by market and changes over time.

**What’s the best way to handle objections?** Acknowledge, investigate, then respond. Most objections hide a more specific concern, and a single diagnostic question usually does more than a scripted rebuttal.

**How do you track objections across a sales team?** Tag every objection by type across all recorded calls and record what each rep did next. Manual tracking samples too few calls to see trends.

**Which objection responses work best?** The honest answer is: the ones associated with better outcomes in your own deals. That’s measurable once every objection and response is tracked.

Page: https://usebylda.com/objection-handling-analysis
